187.t: Professor Claiborne Williams and his big band
187.s: Williams was a violinist who taught every instrument; his sixteen-piece stock-arrangement band played the Pelican roof garden, with his trombonist brother and son George.
187.q: Professor Claiborne Williams had a wonderful band. He came down here to New Orleans and he played on the Pelican roof garden there when it was open. And you couldn't get in there. The people here in New Orleans say that all the larger bands from the north came down and say, but Professor Williams,…

187.t: Williams band style and violin-playing leaders
187.s: The band played stocks and waltzes, not hot jazz; leaders like Williams and Joe Gabriel sat and played violin while trumpeters knocked off.
187.q: No, he didn't use that hot jazz. He just followed the stocks, you understand? And put in some waltzes. He had a beautiful waltz there, what he wrote there for his name, Logical Point. It's just beautiful waltz. That's when his brother used to play that. He used to play it way up above the staff.…

297.t: The Claiborne Williams band: size, style and family
297.s: Claiborne Williams led one of the best bands in the South, a reading orchestra of about 14 with violins; his son George played trumpet and daughter Mary piano.
297.q: Orchestra. They could play all kinds of music. All kinds of music. All kinds of music. He wasn't a fake band. He was a first class band. Used music most of the time.

601.t: Other Algiers dance bands: Tom's, Henry Allen, Kid Thomas, Edmund Payton
601.s: Russell asks about other dance bands across the river. Martin says Tom's was the first; Henry Allen's father played only brass bands, and Kid Thomas and Jack Paeda played dances later. Tom recalls an earlier Edmund Payton band with a left-handed violinist.
601.q: Well, the only bands I remember back there when I was a kid over there was Tom.

188.t: Robichaux and Claiborne Williams bands compared
188.s: He describes Robichaux's orchestra and Williams's band as classical dance music, with simple two-part orchestrations.
188.q: Well, you know, just like the straight orchestration. They didn't have no more than two parts to it, you know, the first and second parts. Yeah. They didn't have no arrangements. Of course, the special arrangement thing didn't start after World War I.

836.t: Dances in Donaldsonville and bands for the children
836.s: Allen asks about dances and bands for the young people at Holy Family; Edna says the sisters wanted the best.
836.q: They had other bands, huh? Not so. I don't know what they called. But I really don't know what they made, but it was a funny little band. You know, one of those little, nobody thought much of them. Just a little. I don't know.

404.t: Claiborne Williams' big band at the dances
404.s: Harold recalls dances in 1929 where the Donaldsonville band of Claiborne Williams, with son George, was hired.
404.q: And after, like they used to give the dancers a long time ago that we know, and they had all the top bands used to come there and play. And like when we'd come in town, that was in 1929 when we'd give a dance and bagged up, and like I said before, they loved Claiborne Williams, some from…

837.s: Robichaux was a polished left-handed violinist whose house band at La Louisiane played from arrangements. He hired hot players such as Perez and Lorenzo Tio Jr., and waltzes came every third or fourth dance.
837.q: Now, Robichaud, to me, he was one of the most polished gentlemen that I ever knew. He was soft-spoken, very well educated, and as we all know, he was a left-hand violinist.
